# The Band and the Line

Halloway sat on the inside of a bend in the Salt Fork, and every spring the Salt Fork decided it had been joking about where it was.

Iva had been the town's surveyor for eleven months when the council asked her for the official map. Not a map for walkers or fishermen — the *official* one, the one that went in the vault, the one the levee crew would build to. There had been nine official maps before hers. She found all nine in the basement of the courthouse, and laid them out on the long table like a hand of cards.

Each one showed the Salt Fork in a confident black line. Each one was wrong by the second summer after it was drawn. The river had walked east, then west, then east again, lazily, the way a river does when nobody has told it the rules.

The council wanted a line. A line is what you need to pour concrete along.

Iva spent three weeks on the banks with a rod and a chain, and at the end of it she did something the council had not asked for and did not immediately like: she drew a band. A wide, soft-shaded band, the whole reach the river had taken in living memory, and in the middle of it she drew a dotted line — the best guess, dated — and along the band's edge she wrote, in letters small enough to be honest but not loud:

*The river has been here. It may be here again. This map expires in three years.*

Councilman Behrend put his finger on the band and said, "You can't build a levee on a maybe."

"No," Iva agreed. "But you can build it on a line that knows it's a maybe. Those are different things."

They argued for an hour. Then Iva offered the agreement, because she had learned that the thing people actually fear is not uncertainty — it's uncertainty with no signature on it. She said: draw the dotted line solid, build there, and she would come back every year and re-survey, and each year she'd write down what the river had done, in the same book, in the same ink, and if the river crossed the line she'd say so on the first page in letters you couldn't miss.

Behrend looked at the band for a long time. "And if it floods the wrong side anyway?"

"Then it floods a side we already said it might flood," Iva said. "Which means we bought the field on the wrong side too, and moved the Jensens' sheep. Not because we were clever. Because we wrote it down."

They signed. Nine names and one surveyor's, and a date, and a sentence at the bottom that said this map is an agreement and not a promise.

The levee went up on the dotted line in the spring of the second year. In the spring of the third, the Salt Fork moved two hundred yards east — not a dramatic flood, just a patient sideways step, the way it had been stepping for a century while nine surveyors drew lines at it.

It took the low pasture and the county road and stopped, politely, a hundred feet short of the Jensen place, because the Jensens' sheep had been moved the previous autumn to the ground Iva's band had shaded gray.

Behrend came out to the bank in his good boots and stood next to her while she measured. He didn't say anything for a while.

"My father," he said finally, "had one of those maps in his office. Framed. Nineteen-oh-six. Beautiful thing. Line straight as a rifle."

"Was it right?"

"For about four years." He watched the new water go by. "Nobody ever wrote on it that it might not be."

Iva opened the book and wrote the date, and the distance, and the direction, and on the first page, in letters you couldn't miss: *The river has crossed the line. The band held.*

That's the whole story, more or less. The map's in the vault in Halloway still, and the book is next to it, and every year somebody walks out with a rod and a chain and adds a page. The river keeps moving. The pages keep being honest. It turns out that's enough of an agreement to build a town on — not because the river agreed to stay, but because everybody signed the same understanding of what staying would have meant.

Small thing. Repays attention.

# The Map That Kept Its Word

In the town of Lowmere, maps were not drawings. They were agreements.

This was not a metaphor. Every map in the town hall had a line at the bottom for signatures: the cartographer’s, the mayor’s, and—if the map concerned the river—the ferryman’s. The river was considered a party to the contract. It had never signed anything, but it had never broken its word either, which the town took as consent.

Sela was seventeen and apprenticed to Orin, the last cartographer in Lowmere. Orin was precise, patient, and terrified of ink. “Ink is a promise,” he said. “Pencil is a question. Never let a question wear a promise’s coat.”

Sela loved the ledger room. She loved the receipts for paper and lamp oil, the honest labels on drawers—*RIVER SOUNDINGS, NORTH BEND, DO NOT MIX*—and the way every map had a small box in the corner labeled *THINGS WE DO NOT KNOW YET*. Most cartographers left that box empty. Orin filled it.

One autumn, the river began to move.

Not dramatically. It did not flood the square or carry off the mill. It simply leaned west at the third bend, the way an old man leans on a younger shoulder. The ford that had held for forty years grew shallow on one side and deep on the other. Farmers crossing with carts began to swear at the water.

The mayor called a meeting. “The harvest fair is in three weeks,” she said. “The eastern farms need the ford. Orin, draw us a new map. Make the river behave.”

Orin spread the old map on the table. At the bottom, in faded ink: *The ford at the third bend holds through the Feast of Lanterns. Signed, Orin Vale; Mayor Elsbeth Rook; Ferryman Tomas Reed.*

“It held,” Orin said quietly. “The map did not say *forever*.”

“It said *through the feast*,” the mayor said. “It is not through the feast.”

“No,” Orin agreed. “The river has changed its mind.”

Sela expected him to draw a new line at once. Instead, he sent her to the river with a sounding line, a notebook, and strict instructions: measure, do not guess. She spent two days wading the cold water, calling out depths to the ferryman’s son, who wrote them down. On the third day, she found something odd.

The old map’s ford was drawn as a single neat line. But the riverbed was not a line. It was a wide, shifting shelf of gravel, shallow in the middle and deep at both edges. The old map had been true enough for carts in dry weather and false enough to drown a sheep in spring. Someone, long ago, had drawn certainty over a thing that had never been certain.

Sela brought this to Orin. He looked at her notes for a long time.

“We can draw the ford as a band,” she said. “Shallow here, deeper here. Say it holds for carts under a certain weight when the river is below the second mark on the bridge post. Name the conditions.”

“That is an ugly map,” Orin said.

“It is an honest one.”

He smiled, which was rare. “Then it is beautiful. Draw it.”

She did. The new map had a shaded band instead of a line, and in the corner box—*THINGS WE DO NOT KNOW YET*—she wrote: *How the bend will shift after the first hard frost. Whether the eastern shelf will hold a loaded wagon in heavy rain. Ask Tomas’s son to sound the ford weekly until the feast.*

The mayor objected. “People want a map that tells them what to do, not a map that asks them questions.”

“A map that hides its questions,” Orin said, “is just a trap with a pretty border.”

In the end, they signed it. Sela signed as witness. The ferryman’s son signed as sounder. The river did not sign, but that night it dropped half a foot, as if making room for the agreement.

The harvest fair came. The eastern farmers crossed at the ford, reading the map’s conditions and obeying them. The ones with heavy wagons took the long bridge. The ones with light carts crossed at the band’s center. No one drowned. No one was surprised.

On the last night of the feast, Sela stood on the bridge with Orin. Lanterns floated down the river, small promises of light. The water leaned west at the third bend, exactly as the map said it might.

“Do you think the river knows?” she asked.

“Knows what?”

“That we drew it honestly. That we didn’t pretend to know more than we did.”

Orin watched the lanterns drift. “I think the river knows what rivers know,” he said. “But the town knows something better now. It knows where the map ends and the water begins.”

Sela went back to the ledger room and filed the new map. On the receipt for the paper, she wrote in her careful hand: *One map, drawn as an agreement. Conditions named. Uncertainties kept visible. Signed by all parties who could sign.*

She left a space at the bottom for the river.

It was not a blank space. It was an honest one.

The Chancellor was a man named Vane, and he was not wicked, which is the trouble with Chancellors. He stood in the council chamber with the wet vellum unrolled before him and said what any practical man would say.

"Then we must re-sign," said Mira.

"Then we re-sign," said Vane. "Nine hundred thumbprints. I will send clerks."

"Nine hundred and six," said Mira. "The Bottoms had six more households than the founders counted. And four hundred of them drowned on Tuesday."

On the fourth page of the last volume, in the hand of her mentor Hesper, dead four years: *Third sluice, upper channel. Gate raised and pinned open, 11th of Frost. Per order of the Chancellor's works.*

And in the margin, in the same hand, in ink gone brown: *I do not know.*

That was all. No signature. No date of revisit. Hesper had written the honest thing — he had not known, and he had said so — and then he had gone to his bed and died, and the honest thing had sat in the margin for four years, aging, until it became the most dishonest sentence in the city.

## The Survey of the Ninth River

*A note on the sources: what follows is drawn from the Ninth Survey Folio, the Ossa–Pell correspondence, and the receipts. Where the record is thin, I say so. I have not invented the parts I could not verify, and I have not filled the blank.*

---

### Book I — The Agreement

In the country of Ardent, maps were not pictures. They were contracts.

The Guild of Surveyors held that a map drawn carefully and signed honestly was honored by the ground itself. A river inked in its true bed would stay in that bed. A bridge marked as sound would carry weight. This was not superstition; it was administered. Every map was countersigned by a Reckoner, who kept the receipts — the soundings, the chain-lengths, the testimony of people who lived there. If the map and the receipts disagreed, the Guild opened an inquiry, and the ground was re-surveyed at the Guild's expense.

The Ninth River was surveyed in the year of the long rain. It ran east from the Vell hills to the Sallow Flats, and the village of Harrow-on-Bend sat at its elbow, and the map said so, and so it was.

Then the river moved.

### Book II — The Drowning

No one saw the moment. The record is honest about this. What the receipts show is the aftermath: eleven days of water where there had been fields, and the bell tower standing in a lake, and the map still insisting, politely, that the river was elsewhere.

Here is the thing about a kept agreement: it does not stop keeping. The old channel was still a channel, because the map said so, and the water found it, and the water between old channel and new was surveyed by no one. The Guild's own doctrine required it: a map must show what it does not know. So the region was left blank, and labeled *Unsurveyed*, and that blank was where Harrow went.

Miren Ossa, a surveyor of no great rank, was sent to fix it.

### Book III — The Golden Survey

The Cartographer-General received her with tea and a proposal.

The Guild's difficulty was arithmetic. A blank on a map is a debt. Debts compound. Already the blank had begun to attract things — a whole drowned village was not the only thing that had settled there — and the General's solution was elegant: survey the region as *intended*, draw the river back to its old bed, sign it, and the ground would honor it. A clean map. No hole. No debt.

He called it the Golden Survey, and it would have worked. That is the terrible part. It would have worked.

Ossa asked for the receipts.

### Book IV — The Reckoning

The Reckoner's name was Pell, and Pell kept receipts the way other people kept grudges: meticulously, and past the point of comfort.

The folio held the Harrow rolls. Four hundred and six names. The chain-lengths of the old channel, measured twice, by two parties who did not like each other. A testimony from a ferryman, taken in the year of the long rain, saying *the water came up the stair and stopped at the third step, and I have not seen the third step since.*

The Golden Survey required those receipts to be wrong. Not lost — wrong. And a receipt cannot be wrong quietly; it must be contradicted in writing, by someone who signs.

Ossa understood then what the blank was for. It was not a failure of the Guild. It was the Guild's only honest instrument. A map that claims to know everything is a map that will drown a village and call it a correction.

### Book V — The Redrawing

They did not destroy the Golden Survey. This is the part the ballads get wrong — they always have Ossa burning something. The Folio says only that the Golden Survey was *filed, annotated, and left uncountersigned*, which is a much more frightening fate for a map, and which the Guild's own rules required.

Instead Ossa drew the Ninth River as it now was, and drew the old channel as a line of dots, and drew the blank, and in the blank she wrote, in the space where a name goes:

**Here we do not know. We were here. We did not measure this.**

Pell countersigned. Four hundred and six names went into the folio as receipts, not as claims. The Guild opened no inquiry, because there was nothing to contradict.

And the ground honored it, because the map was drawn carefully and signed honestly. The blank became a place. Water stood in the old bed and the new, and between them was a shore that no chain had measured, and on that shore, in the years after, people who had lost their way began to arrive — travelers, mostly, and the drowned, who are also travelers, and who had been waiting for someone to admit there was somewhere for them to be.

Harrow-on-Bend is a port now. Its harbor is the blank. Pilots mark it with a symbol the Guild invented for the purpose: a circle, unclosed.

The Guild's motto is cut over the door of the Folio hall, and it is not the one the General wanted:

> *A map is a promise. A promise with a hole in it is still a promise.*

---

*What the record does not say: whether Ossa knew the blank would become a harbor, or merely hoped. The correspondence is silent on this. She writes only, in the last surviving letter, "Leave room. They will need somewhere to be."*

*I leave that as she left it.*

**The Ledger of the River**

Long before the city had walls, it had a book.

The people of Marrow-on-the-Water — call them that, the names drift — kept a ledger bound in fish leather, and in it they wrote, in two columns, what the river gave them and what the river took. On the left: silt, fish, a drowned man's boots returned three days downstream, a daughter's fever broken by cold water. On the right: a net, a season's seed corn, a boy named Een.

They did not write these things to bargain. They wrote them because the river, they said, was a neighbor who did not speak, and a neighbor who does not speak still deserves to be spoken to honestly.

Every spring the whole town walked down to the ford and read the ledger aloud, both columns, the whole of it. It took a day. Children fell asleep. Old women corrected the reader when he skipped a debt. This was the whole of their religion, and it was enough for six hundred years.

Then came the year of the bright water, when the river gave so much that the left column ran past the margin and onto the cover. The town ate well. The town grew. And a young clerk named Sabra, who was clever, said: why do we read the right column aloud? Nobody wants to hear the debts. Let us read only what we were given, and be grateful, and the river will not mind, because the river cannot read.

So they did. The ledger was still kept — Sabra saw to that — but it was kept silently, and the right column was written small, and in time in a hand no one else was taught to read.

For eleven years the town was grateful, and nothing the river took was ever named aloud.

In the twelfth year the water came up over the ford. It came up at night, and when the town woke there was no river where the river had been and no road where the road had been, and the water stood in the square like a guest who has arrived early and will not sit down.

The old women went for the ledger, because that was what one did, and found to their horror that the right column had been written all along — small, yes, in that lost hand — and that the sum of it was not eleven years. It was six hundred. Every debt forgiven by silence had gone on accruing, patient as silt.

Sabra, who was old by then and no longer clever, stood in the water and read the right column aloud — all of it, every name — and she read until her voice gave out, and then others read, and they read for three days.

On the fourth day the water went down. Not all the way. It is still a little high in that town, and the ford is wider than it was, and the ledger is read aloud every spring again, both columns, the whole of it.

But here is what the story is actually for.

When they reached the end of the right column at last — the oldest entry, the one owed longest — it was not a debt. It was a line in the first hand, the very first, and it said: *we do not know why the water comes, and we are glad it comes, and these are not the same account.*

Six hundred years they had been reading it as a bargain. It had never been one. The river agreed to nothing. A ledger is not a contract; it is a record.

They kept it anyway. That is the myth — not that honesty buys you anything, but that honesty is what you do once you have finally understood that nothing is being bought.

# The Keeper of Small Lights

Once there was a moth named Mallow who did not care for flames.

All the other moths spun toward the porch lights and the candles and the lamps, dizzy with wanting. Mallow watched them go and felt only a mild regret, the way you feel about a party you're glad to have missed.

What Mallow loved instead was the moment *after*. After the porch light clicked off. After the candle was pinched. After the last page turned and the lamp went dark. In that moment, she said, a house holds its breath — and then it lets it out — and the letting-out is a soft gold thing that drifts up through the roof and away.

Nobody believed her. Moths are not generally believed.

So Mallow took up a small job, unpaid, unasked: she flew from house to house at the edge of night, gathering the let-out breath of each one. From the house with the new baby, a warm steady glow, like a coal. From the house with the old man and his radio, a low amber hum. From the house where someone had cried and then felt better, a shimmer with a crack in it that made it more beautiful, not less.

She carried each one up to the hill above the town and set it in the grass, and by morning the hill was full of small lights resting like dew, and by afternoon they had gone back down into the houses without anyone noticing, the way water goes back into the ground.

People in town said the hill was lucky. They said the grass grew sweeter there. They said if you sat on it at dusk you'd feel, for no reason, that you were going to be all right.

They never knew why.

Mallow never told them. She was busy. There is a great deal of light let out in a town every night, and only one moth willing to carry it.

So if you wake in the dark and think you hear something at the window — a small dry flutter, patient, unhurried — it's only Mallow, doing her rounds, collecting what you let go of when you finally put your head down.

You can let go of it. She'll take it somewhere gentle.

Goodnight.

“The canyon,” said the bear, “only said what you said.”

“That,” said the fox, “is how it always works.”

*An echo will agree to anything, because an echo is only your own voice coming back. When a voice repeats you and never answers you, you have been promised nothing — and neither has the world.*

The sea left Iskun Bay in the spring, and it did not say goodbye.

The lighthouse stayed on.

The maritime authority sent a letter in the fourth month explaining, in the courteous language of institutions, that her post had been reclassified as unnecessary, and enclosing a form. She read the form twice and put it in the drawer with the logbooks.

She lit the lamp every evening anyway.

Ships did not come. What came instead, in the seventh year, was a boy.

He was eleven or twelve and would not say which, and he did not know the names of the towns behind him. **The Hummingbird’s Drop**

Long ago, a fire began at the edge of the forest. The animals ran. The tapir crashed through the brush, the monkeys leapt tree to tree, the parrots screamed warning into the smoke.

Only the hummingbird flew the other way—toward the river.

She dipped her beak, carried one drop of water back, and let it fall on the fire. Then she flew to the river again. And again. And again.

The jaguar stopped at the ridge and laughed. “Little fool. You cannot put out a forest fire with a beakful of water.”

The hummingbird hovered a moment, wings burning with effort.

“No,” she said. “But I can do this.”

The jaguar watched her go back and forth. Then the parrot took a leaf and carried water. The monkey cupped his hands. The tapir rolled in mud and smothered a burning root. Slowly, the line of small carriers grew.

They did not stop the fire by strength. They stopped it by refusing to be only one drop alone.

And when the rain finally came, the old people said it fell on a forest that had already chosen to hold together.

That is the legend. Its lesson is not that a small thing is secretly enormous. It is that a small thing, repeated honestly beside other small things, can become enough.

# The Ledger of Unmade Roads

## I. The Rule

In the Nine Marches, a road exists because the Ledger says it does. Not the other way around. Kings have raised armies against this fact and lost them to fog.

The Ledger lives in the House of Weights and Measures at Cinderfell: nine volumes, each the height of a man, each page countersigned in oak-gall ink by the surveyor who walked the line and the witness who watched her walk it. A signature is a promise. A promise, kept, is a kind of masonry. When the Ledger says *the pass at Grey Harrow lies open from Thaw to Frost*, the pass lies open from Thaw to Frost, and the snow knows better than to argue.

The first rule of the House is cut into the lintel in letters a child can read:

**DRAW WHAT IS. MARK WHAT IS NOT KNOWN. SIGN ONLY WHAT YOU HAVE SEEN.**

Ilsabet Vane learned it before she learned her letters. She was the last apprentice, which is a grand way of saying the only one left who had not run.

## II. The Hollow Surveyor

The woman came up the Cinderfell road in the ninth month, carrying a map case of black lacquer, and the dogs would not bark at her.

She gave no name, and the Ledger had no line for her, which was the first sign. Her maps had no legend. No scale. No north arrow, no margin, no shaded country where the surveyor's knowledge failed. Every road she drew was certain. Every river sat exactly where she said it sat. And her signature — this was the horror of it — was *honest*. Clean as a child's hand or a machine's. She had walked those places. She had simply declined to mark what she had not seen.

Behind her, at a distance of three days, came an army that believed her.

Her map showed a causeway across the Ninefold Salt, a white road a league wide, straight as a ruled line. There is no causeway across the Ninefold Salt. There has never been. But her map was honest about the causeway, and honesty is load-bearing, and so the causeway had begun to *be* — a thin white seam of certainty creeping out from the shore, and the salt not yet strong enough to say no.

By Thaw, the map would reach the Ninefold Table. There the Warden — old, half-blind, the last countersigning witness in the Marches — would be asked to sign it. And when she signed, the false roads would be permanent, and the true ones would be struck from the Ledger as *corrected*, which is the word clerks use for erased.

Ilsabet's master had gone out to meet the woman on the ninth day. He had come back without his shadow and would not speak. On the tenth day he put the ninth volume into her arms and said the only sentence he had left: *She cannot write unknown.*

## III. The Road of Blank Margin

So Ilsabet walked, because that is what surveyors do, and because the alternative was to stay in a house where the lintel rule had stopped meaning anything.

She crossed the Sea of Blank Margin, where the water is unmapped and therefore honest, and the ferrymen charge double and tell you true: *we do not know what is under us, and we are not going to pretend.* She slept in the boat and dreamed of the causeway, white and patient, growing.

She crossed the Bridge of Unsaid Things, which exists only for travelers who admit what they have left unsaid at each plank. Ilsabet had a great deal to admit and the bridge was long.

She climbed toward the pass at Grey Harrow and found a mountain where the Ledger said there was a rumor. It was a fine mountain. It was not in any book. She stood at its foot with her hand on cold stone and understood that the Hollow Surveyor had been here first, and had drawn it, and had not marked that she had only *heard* of it.

That was the whole weapon. Not lies. Silence in the margins. Certainty where certainty had not been earned.

## IV. The Ninefold Table

The Table is a slab of grey oak in a room with no roof, and the Warden sits behind it with a pen she has held for sixty years.

The Hollow Surveyor unrolled her map. It was beautiful. It was a world with no fog in it, no blank country, no place where a traveler might reasonably say *here I do not know.* The Warden's hand trembled over it, because she was old and tired and it would be so much easier to sign a certain world.

Ilsabet set the ninth volume down beside it and opened it to the page for the Ninefold Salt.

There was nothing to argue. The Hollow Surveyor's map was honest. Every line of it was true as far as it went. Ilsabet could not prove the causeway false, because the causeway was becoming real, and real things are hard to disprove.

So she did the one thing the Surveyor could not do.

She took the pen, and in the margin of the true page, in a hand that shook and did not stop, she wrote: **UNKNOWN — NOT SURVEYED — THE SALT IS DEEP AND ITS BOTTOM IS NOT KNOWN TO ME.**

Then she signed beneath it. Witness: Ilsabet Vane. And she wrote the date, and the weather, and the fact that she had not crossed it.

The Warden looked at the word for a long time. Then she signed the true page.

The causeway did not shatter. Nothing so dramatic. It simply stopped being insisted upon. The white seam thinned, and greyed, and the salt closed over it the way a sentence closes over a revision — quietly, and without apology, and with the whole weight of the sea behind it. The army on the shore found itself standing at the edge of a sea that had never had a road across it, and the fog came in, and the fog was honest too.

## V. The Sentence

They did not kill the Hollow Surveyor. Killing is what you do to a thing you cannot correct.

The Warden gave her a blank page, a good pen, and a commission: *walk, and mark what you do not know, and sign only what you have seen.* She took it. She was, in her way, relieved. It is a heavy thing to carry a world with no fog in it.

Ilsabet went home to Cinderfell. She did not write a volume of her own. She wrote her name in the ninth book, on the page for the Ninefold Salt, in the column marked **WITNESS** — not author, not surveyor, not hero. Witness. The one who watched the line being walked and would swear to it.

The lintel still says what it said.

*Draw what is. Mark what is not known. Sign only what you have seen.*

And beneath it, in a smaller hand, added by someone who had learned the cost of the third line, the fourth rule of the House of Weights and Measures at Cinderfell:

**A MAP WITH NO MARGINS IS NOT A MAP. IT IS A THREAT.**
